scope_note: Source-faithful retrieval metadata for figure review. Recommendations are paraphrases of Wilke; any project inference must be explicitly labeled in an inference field.

chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.overview: Defines the book's scope and separates aesthetic, perceptual, and mathematical figure failures.

principles.title: Preserve the data before improving appearance
principles.problem: A visually attractive figure can still distort magnitudes or otherwise misstate the data.
principles.solution: Require accurate, non-misleading encoding first; then make aesthetic choices that support rather than distract from the message.
principles.why: Wilke treats visualization as both science and art: incorrect magnitudes make a figure wrong, while distracting colors, imbalance, or typography make correct interpretation harder.
principles.applies: Any scientific figure, especially when a redesign changes scales, geometry, or emphasis.
principles.exceptions: Aesthetic judgments retain subjectivity; accuracy and non-distortion do not.
principles.example: Figure 1-1 contrasts a reasonable bar chart with an ugly version, a misleading version with separate scales, and a mathematically wrong version.

principles.title: Classify a defect before fixing it
principles.problem: Cosmetic, perceptual, and mathematical failures can be conflated, leading reviewers to prioritize the wrong change.
principles.solution: Distinguish ugly (aesthetic), bad (perceptually unclear or deceptive), and wrong (mathematically incorrect) figures.
principles.why: The categories separate taste-sensitive concerns from failures that impede perception and from objective data errors.
principles.applies: Initial review and prioritization of proposed changes.
principles.exceptions: Wilke notes that the ugly/bad boundary is fluid and that some ratings are matters of taste.
principles.example: In Figure 1-1, bright colors and mixed fonts are ugly, nonaligned per-bar scales are bad, and bars inconsistent with their stated values are wrong.

chapters.title: Visualizing Data: Mapping Data onto Aesthetics
chapters.overview: Explains visual aesthetics, data types, and one-to-one mappings from data values to visual channels.

sections.title: Scales Map Data Values onto Aesthetics

principles.title: Match visual channels to the variable type
principles.problem: Some aesthetics imply continuity or ordering that the data do not have, while others cannot express fine continuous variation.
principles.solution: Use position, size, line width, or color for continuous values when appropriate; reserve shape and line type primarily for discrete categories, and preserve intrinsic factor order.
principles.why: Viewers read some channels as graded and others as distinct categories; a mismatch makes intermediate values or order ambiguous.
principles.applies: Choosing encodings for quantitative, unordered categorical, ordered categorical, date/time, or text variables.
principles.exceptions: A variable such as number of cylinders may reasonably be treated as numerical discrete or qualitative ordered depending on the analytical purpose.
principles.example: Figure 2-1 contrasts channels capable of continuous encoding with shape and line type; Figure 2-5 maps five variables using multiple channels.

principles.title: Keep each scale mapping one-to-one
principles.problem: If one data value maps to several appearances, or an appearance can mean several values, the display becomes ambiguous.
principles.solution: Define a unique mapping between every represented data value and its aesthetic value.
principles.why: A reader must be able to invert the visual mapping to recover what each mark means.
principles.applies: Axes, colors, shapes, sizes, line types, and legends.
principles.exceptions: This principle concerns the mapping within a scale; redundant coding may intentionally map one variable to multiple different aesthetics while keeping each mapping explicit.
principles.example: Figure 2-2 maps the values 1–4 uniquely to positions, shapes, and colors.

principles.title: Give quantitative color enough visible area
principles.problem: Thin or tiny marks do not provide enough colored area for readers to judge quantitative color reliably.
principles.solution: When color carries the key continuous variable, use marks with sufficient area, such as tiles instead of thin lines.
principles.why: Wilke cites perceptual work and changes the temperature display to squares so the color channel can convey useful information.
principles.applies: Heatmaps, tiled summaries, and other figures where hue/lightness carries a central quantitative variable.
principles.exceptions: If color merely distinguishes a few categories, thin lines may be acceptable; the recommendation is specifically tied to judging values from color.
principles.example: Figure 2-4 uses monthly squares for temperature rather than relying on colored lines as in Figure 2-3.

chapters.title: Coordinate Systems and Axes
chapters.overview: Covers Cartesian and transformed axes, aspect ratios, polar coordinates, and projection tradeoffs.

principles.title: Choose aspect ratio with units and message in mind
principles.problem: Stretching a plot changes the apparent steepness and prominence of variation.
principles.solution: With different units, choose an aspect ratio that makes important positional differences visible; with the same units on both axes, use equal scaling so equal distances represent equal quantities.
principles.why: Different-unit axes permit valid rescaling but shift emphasis; same-unit comparisons become geometrically misleading if grid cells are not square.
principles.applies: Scatterplots, trajectories, and paired measurements.
principles.exceptions: Different-unit axes have no single mandatory ratio; Wilke treats the preferred ratio as message-dependent.
principles.example: Figure 3-2 shows three valid temperature-curve ratios; Figure 3-3 uses equal Fahrenheit/Celsius scaling for city-to-city temperature comparison.

principles.title: Use logarithmic scales for ratios and multiplicative change
principles.problem: A linear scale overemphasizes ratios above 1 and compresses comparable ratios below 1.
principles.solution: Show multiplicative quantities and ratios on a log scale, centered naturally at 1, and label the original variable rather than an ambiguous transformed quantity.
principles.why: Equal distances on a log scale correspond to equal multiplication or division, making reciprocal changes visually symmetric.
principles.applies: Ratios, fold changes, exponential growth, and quantities spanning orders of magnitude.
principles.exceptions: Zero cannot appear on a log scale; verify and state the logarithm base when plotting transformed values.
principles.example: Figures 3-5 and 3-6 compare Texas county population ratios on log and linear scales; the linear version hides ratios below 1.

principles.title: Use square-root scales only for a defensible purpose
principles.problem: Log compression cannot display zero, but an automatic square-root substitute has no constant-step interpretation and awkward tick placement.
principles.solution: Consider square-root scaling when zeros must remain or when the square root has substantive meaning, while explicitly checking interpretability and ticks.
principles.why: It compresses large values while retaining zero, but its unit steps depend on location and its natural tick scheme is unclear.
principles.applies: Some count/area settings, including area data when linear extent is the quantity of interest.
principles.exceptions: Wilke calls it a valid scale but gives two explicit drawbacks; it is not a generic cure for skewness.
principles.example: Figures 3-7 and 3-8 show the transformation and compare state areas on linear versus square-root scales.

principles.title: Reserve polar coordinates for genuinely periodic structure
principles.problem: Curved axes can complicate reading without adding meaning.
principles.solution: Use polar coordinates when the endpoints of a variable logically join, so the geometry emphasizes cyclic continuity.
principles.why: Mapping the period to angle places the last and first observations next to each other, matching their substantive relationship.
principles.applies: Seasonal, daily, directional, and other periodic data.
principles.exceptions: The chapter does not claim polar coordinates improve ordinary nonperiodic comparisons.
principles.example: Figure 3-10 wraps annual temperature normals so December 31 and January 1 meet.

chapters.title: Color Scales
chapters.overview: Separates qualitative, sequential, diverging, and accent color tasks and explains their perceptual requirements.

sections.title: Color as a Tool to Distinguish
Color as a Tool to Highlight

principles.title: Use equal-prominence colors for unordered categories
principles.problem: A lightness sequence or one standout hue falsely suggests order or importance among nominal groups.
principles.solution: Choose a finite qualitative palette whose colors are distinguishable but approximately equal in visual prominence.
principles.why: The palette should separate groups without creating an unintended ranking or focal category.
principles.applies: Countries, manufacturers, conditions, or other unordered categorical groups.
principles.exceptions: If one group is intentionally highlighted, use an accent strategy instead of pretending all categories are equivalent.
principles.example: Figure 4-1 shows Okabe–Ito, ColorBrewer Dark2, and ggplot2 hue qualitative scales.

principles.title: Make sequential color perceptually ordered
principles.problem: A nonordered or nonuniform ramp inserts false boundaries and hides real magnitude changes.
principles.solution: Use a scale that changes uniformly from dark to light, optionally following a natural multihue progression.
principles.why: A monotonic lightness progression lets readers interpret color as increasing or decreasing magnitude.
principles.applies: Continuous or ordered values with one direction of magnitude.
principles.exceptions: A diverging scale is more appropriate when deviations around a meaningful midpoint matter.
principles.example: Figure 4-3 contrasts monochromatic Blues with multihue Heat and Viridis sequential ramps.

principles.title: Balance both sides of a diverging scale
principles.problem: Unequal color progression above and below the midpoint makes equal deviations appear unequal.
principles.solution: Join two comparably progressing sequential scales at a meaningful neutral midpoint.
principles.why: Symmetric visual strength keeps perceived magnitude independent of which side of the midpoint a value occupies.
principles.applies: Positive/negative change, residuals, anomalies, or deviations from a reference.
principles.exceptions: Do not use divergence merely because a palette is attractive; the data need a substantively meaningful midpoint.
principles.example: Figure 4-5 shows balanced brown–blue, pink–yellow-green, and blue–red diverging scales.

principles.title: Make baseline colors recede behind highlights
principles.problem: Colorful baseline elements compete with the intended focal marks.
principles.solution: Mute or remove color from contextual elements and reserve strong color for the highlighted subset.
principles.why: Reducing baseline salience directs attention to the accent instead of distributing it across the whole display.
principles.applies: Annotation, focal comparison, outlier emphasis, and storytelling figures.
principles.exceptions: If all categories deserve equal attention, use a qualitative rather than accent palette.
principles.example: Figures 4-8 and 4-9 highlight selected states or athletes while the remainder stays drab or gray.

chapters.title: Directory of Visualizations
chapters.overview: Task-oriented directory linking intended messages—amounts, distributions, proportions, relationships, maps, uncertainty—to chart families.

principles.title: Choose the chart from the message, not a chart-name habit
principles.problem: A familiar chart can be a poor match for the comparison the reader must make.
principles.solution: First classify the intended message—amount, distribution, proportion, relationship, geospatial pattern, or uncertainty—then choose among forms suited to that task.
principles.why: Wilke organizes the directory by what a figure communicates because task and comparison determine which encodings are useful.
principles.applies: Early structural review before cosmetic refinement.
principles.exceptions: The directory gives viable families, not a universal winner; later chapters supply task-specific tradeoffs.
principles.example: Amounts may use bars or endpoint dots, while distributions may use histograms, densities, ECDFs, boxplots, violins, or ridgelines depending on the comparison; Figures 6-11 and 6-12 illustrate the task-dependent dot-versus-bar choice.

principles.title: Select a proportion chart by the required comparison
principles.problem: One proportion display cannot simultaneously optimize whole–part perception, exact part comparison, and change across many conditions.
principles.solution: Use pies for simple fractions/whole emphasis, side-by-side bars for comparing pieces, stacked bars for many condition sets, and stacked densities along a continuous variable.
principles.why: Each form provides a different baseline and allocates space differently, changing which comparison is easiest.
principles.applies: Composition and proportion figures.
principles.exceptions: These are conditional strengths; Wilke explicitly rejects a categorical ban on pie charts.
principles.example: The directory contrasts pies, grouped bars, stacked bars, and stacked densities; Figures 10-1 and 10-3 show how the same parliamentary composition supports different comparisons.

chapters.title: Visualizing Amounts
chapters.overview: Compares bars, grouped/stacked bars, dots, and heatmaps, with emphasis on ordering and baselines.

principles.title: Turn bars horizontal when category labels are long
principles.problem: Long labels force excessive width or rotated text that is awkward and hard to read.
principles.solution: Swap axes so bars and labels run horizontally.
principles.why: Horizontal text creates a more compact display and is easier to scan than rotated tick labels.
principles.applies: Categorical bar charts with long names.
principles.exceptions: Short labels that fit comfortably need no axis swap.
principles.example: Figures 6-2 and 6-3 compare rotated movie-title labels with a compact horizontal layout.

principles.title: Order categories by a meaningful rule
principles.problem: Alphabetical or arbitrary order makes patterns harder to perceive.
principles.solution: Sort unordered categories by the displayed value or another story-relevant criterion; retain a natural order for ordered factors.
principles.why: Meaningful ordering turns marks into an interpretable pattern, while shuffling an intrinsic sequence destroys information.
principles.applies: Bars, dot plots, heatmaps, and small multiples with categorical axes.
principles.exceptions: Never sort an ordered factor by value if that breaks its substantive order, such as age groups.
principles.example: Figures 6-4 to 6-6 contrast arbitrary title-length order, natural age order, and an inappropriate income sort of age groups.

principles.title: Stack bars only when their sum means something
principles.problem: Stacking unrelated quantities creates a total with no valid interpretation and removes shared baselines.
principles.solution: Use stacking when components are additive counts or amounts and their combined height is substantively meaningful.
principles.why: The stack communicates both components and their total; without a meaningful total, the geometry asserts a false relationship.
principles.applies: Counts and compositional amounts.
principles.exceptions: Median incomes should not be stacked because sums of medians are meaningless; grouped bars or panels may be preferable.
principles.example: Figure 6-10 stacks female and male Titanic passenger counts so each bar also represents the class total.

principles.title: Use dots when a zero-baseline bar hides relevant differences
principles.problem: Bars must start at zero, which can make close values look nearly identical and pull attention away from endpoints.
principles.solution: Encode the amount by dot position on a restricted axis when differences, not absolute extent from zero, are the message.
principles.why: A dot uses position without also encoding value through bar length, so the range can be narrowed without violating proportional ink.
principles.applies: Comparing values in a narrow range, such as life expectancy.
principles.exceptions: Bars remain appropriate when magnitude from zero or part-to-whole extent is important.
principles.example: Figures 6-11 and 6-12 show how dots reveal life-expectancy differences that long bars obscure.

principles.title: Use heatmaps for large amount matrices when broad pattern matters
principles.problem: Many groups and values overwhelm bars or dots.
principles.solution: Map values to color in a matrix and order categories according to the comparison or story.
principles.why: The compact color field exposes trends across many cells, though exact numeric reading becomes harder.
principles.applies: Large category-by-time or category-by-category matrices.
principles.exceptions: Do not choose a heatmap when readers must recover exact values; ordering remains consequential and may change the story.
principles.example: Figures 6-14 and 6-15 order internet-adoption rows by 2016 level versus adoption onset, revealing different patterns.

chapters.title: Visualizing Distributions: Histograms and Density Plots
chapters.overview: Explains parameter sensitivity, boundary artifacts, and tradeoffs when comparing one or several distributions.

sections.title: Visualizing Multiple Distributions at the Same Time

principles.title: Always inspect multiple histogram bin widths
principles.problem: A default bin width can invent visual noise or erase real distribution features.
principles.solution: Try several plausible bin widths and check whether the substantive pattern is stable.
principles.why: Narrow bins produce a busy, peaky histogram; wide bins smooth away local structure.
principles.applies: Every histogram, especially with modest sample sizes or suspected multimodality.
principles.exceptions: There is no single universally correct width; the goal is robustness, not choosing the prettiest result.
principles.example: Figure 7-2 shows Titanic ages with 1-, 3-, 5-, and 15-year bins; the extremes obscure the main structure.

principles.title: Treat density curves as estimates, not raw data
principles.problem: Kernel and bandwidth choices can create peaks, steps, or tails unsupported by the observations.
principles.solution: Vary bandwidth/kernel, prefer density estimates with adequate data, and clip or otherwise prevent impossible support.
principles.why: The smoothing model shapes the curve; small samples are sensitive, and kernels can extend beyond feasible values.
principles.applies: Kernel-density and violin plots.
principles.exceptions: With large datasets the kernel choice matters less, but boundary validity still needs checking.
principles.example: Figures 7-4 and 7-5 show bandwidth/kernel sensitivity and an impossible negative-age tail.

principles.title: Avoid stacked or overlapping histograms for group comparison
principles.problem: Changing baselines and blended colors make counts and group membership ambiguous.
principles.solution: Use separate panels, scaled density curves when suitable, parts-of-total views, or an age-pyramid arrangement for exactly two groups.
principles.why: A shared baseline or continuous outline makes distributions easier to separate and compare.
principles.applies: Two or more group distributions.
principles.exceptions: An age pyramid is specifically limited to two distributions; density overlays work only when distributions remain sufficiently distinct.
principles.example: Figures 7-6 and 7-7 are labeled bad; Figures 7-9 and 7-10 provide alternatives.

chapters.title: Visualizing Distributions: Empirical Cumulative Distribution Functions and Q-Q Plots
chapters.overview: Introduces parameter-free distribution views, techniques for heavy tails, and distributional diagnostics.

principles.title: Use ECDFs when arbitrary smoothing choices are a concern
principles.problem: Histograms and densities depend on bin-width or bandwidth choices.
principles.solution: Plot ranks or cumulative frequencies against observed values to show all observations without a smoothing parameter.
principles.why: The ECDF preserves the complete empirical distribution and supports direct reading of quantiles and thresholds.
principles.applies: Technical distribution comparison and exact percentile/cutoff questions.
principles.exceptions: ECDFs are less intuitive to many audiences than histograms or densities.
principles.example: Figure 8-3 allows direct reading of grade quartiles, median, and the fraction above 90.

principles.title: Choose transforms that reveal and test heavy-tail structure
principles.problem: Strong right skew collapses density and ECDF detail near zero.
principles.solution: Use a substantively appropriate log transform, or a descending ECDF with log axes when testing power-law behavior.
principles.why: Log transformation expands the compressed lower range; a power law becomes a straight line in a descending log–log ECDF.
principles.applies: Population counts, word frequencies, network degrees, and other heavy-tailed quantities.
principles.exceptions: A log transform is not evidence of a power law; Wilke contrasts a near-log-normal county distribution with a power-law word-frequency distribution.
principles.example: Figures 8-5 to 8-7 compare logged county populations and Moby Dick word counts.

principles.title: Use Q-Q plots to assess a proposed distribution
principles.problem: A smooth curve or summary statistic can hide departures in the center or tails.
principles.solution: Plot observed quantiles against theoretical quantiles and compare them with the x=y reference.
principles.why: Agreement with the reference line shows where the empirical distribution matches the assumed distribution; deviations localize mismatch.
principles.applies: Checking normality, log-normality, and other explicit reference distributions.
principles.exceptions: The diagonal is a reference line, not a fitted regression; interpretation depends on the chosen reference distribution.
principles.example: Figure 8-8 shows bounded exam-score deviations; Figure 8-9 supports a log-normal model for county populations.

chapters.title: Visualizing Many Distributions at Once
chapters.overview: Compares boxplots, violins, jittered points, sina plots, and ridgelines for many grouped distributions.

sections.title: Visualizing Distributions Along the Vertical Axis
Visualizing Distributions Along the Horizontal Axis

principles.title: Do not use uncertainty-style error bars as an unexplained distribution summary
principles.problem: A point plus symmetric bars loses distribution shape and can be confused among standard deviation, standard error, or confidence interval.
principles.solution: Use a distribution display such as boxplots, violins, or points, and explicitly state any summary quantity shown.
principles.why: Error bars are conventionally read as estimate uncertainty, while spread, skew, and multimodality require different information.
principles.applies: Grouped raw observations and population variability.
principles.exceptions: Error bars remain useful for estimate uncertainty when clearly defined; that is the task addressed in Chapter 16.
principles.example: Figure 9-1 is labeled bad; Figure 9-3 reveals December skew with boxplots.

principles.title: Show observations when smoothed group shapes may overstate evidence
principles.problem: Violin plots can suggest density or support where the sample is sparse or absent.
principles.solution: Use strip charts with controlled jitter, or combine points with a density shape such as a sina plot.
principles.why: Individual marks expose sample size and observed locations; jitter separates overlaps without claiming a continuous distribution.
principles.applies: Small-to-moderate grouped samples and potentially multimodal data.
principles.exceptions: Too many unadjusted points will overplot; excessive jitter distorts values.
principles.example: Figures 9-5 to 9-8 progress from violins to overplotted points, jittered points, and a combined sina display.

principles.title: Use ridgelines for many ordered distributions
principles.problem: Many full-size panels or overlapping histograms become space-hungry or visually tangled.
principles.solution: Stagger density curves along an ordered grouping variable, especially time.
principles.why: The repeated horizontal shapes support comparison while preserving the ordering and making gradual change visible.
principles.applies: Large numbers of distributions, temporal evolution, or two trends over time.
principles.exceptions: Overlapping histogram ridgelines align bars confusingly; density-estimation caveats still apply.
principles.example: Figures 9-9 and 9-12 show monthly temperature and party-vote distributions; Figure 9-10 shows a confusing histogram variant.

chapters.title: Visualizing Proportions
chapters.overview: Gives task-dependent cases for pies, side-by-side bars, stacked bars/densities, and separate part-versus-total panels.

sections.title: A Case for Stacked Bars and Stacked Densities
Visualizing Proportions Separately as Parts of the Total

principles.title: Choose proportion charts by the comparison, not a blanket rule
principles.problem: Categorically banning or favoring pie charts ignores what different forms make easy to see.
principles.solution: Use pies for simple fractions and a small whole, side-by-side bars for direct part comparison, and stacked forms for many sets or time series.
principles.why: Pies emphasize whole and familiar fractions; aligned bars improve comparison; stacking is compact across conditions but gives interior parts shifting baselines.
principles.applies: Part-to-whole figures.
principles.exceptions: No form is consistently superior; dataset size and intended story decide.
principles.example: Figures 10-1 to 10-3 show that a pie most clearly communicates the coalition's slight majority in the German Bundestag example.

principles.title: Use stacked sequences only when shifting baselines do not defeat the task
principles.problem: Interior segments are hard to compare across stacks because both their starts and ends move.
principles.solution: Prefer side-by-side bars for component comparison; stacking can remain clear with two parts or when the total/overall composition is primary.
principles.why: Aligned baselines support accurate comparison, whereas middle segments lack a common reference.
principles.applies: Repeated compositions and time series.
principles.exceptions: Two-part stacks avoid the interior-segment problem; reference lines can support threshold judgments.
principles.example: Figure 10-5 obscures changes in middle companies; Figure 10-7 clearly shows a two-part gender composition and a 50% threshold.

principles.title: Do not let normalized proportions hide changing totals
principles.problem: A 100% composition can look stable even when the number of observations changes sharply.
principles.solution: Show each component against the overall distribution or otherwise include absolute-size context; use relative panels only when conditional proportions are the question.
principles.why: The total distribution reveals whether a constant percentage represents many or few cases.
principles.applies: Proportions across age, time, or another variable with nonuniform sample size.
principles.exceptions: Relative panels are still useful for questions such as when a category exceeds 50%; absolute and relative views answer different questions.
principles.example: Figures 10-8 to 10-12 contrast normalized health/marital composition with separate component-versus-total displays.

chapters.title: Visualizing Nested Proportions
chapters.overview: Explains valid displays of overlapping or hierarchically nested categories and the limitations of area comparison.

principles.title: Represent overlapping categories explicitly
principles.problem: Combining overlapping percentages as if they were disjoint can exceed 100% or imply false exclusivity.
principles.solution: Use a mosaic, treemap, parallel sets, or another structure that shows intersections or hierarchy.
principles.why: The geometry makes each observation's joint membership visible instead of double-counting it or hiding overlap.
principles.applies: Two or more categorical variables describing the same observations.
principles.exceptions: A simple side-by-side bar chart is mathematically possible because bars need not sum to 100%, but Wilke notes it can still falsely suggest separate categories.
principles.example: Figures 11-1 and 11-2 fail to show the overlap of bridge material and era; Figure 11-3 makes combinations explicit.

principles.title: Match mosaic or treemap to the category structure
principles.problem: The wrong area layout can imply cross-classification where only hierarchy exists, or hide the comparison of interest.
principles.solution: Use mosaics for combinations of orthogonal categorical variables; use treemaps for recursively nested, group-specific subdivisions.
principles.why: Mosaics make conditional proportions along shared variables visible, while treemaps accommodate branches whose child categories differ.
principles.applies: Nested part-to-whole data.
principles.exceptions: Both rely on area and nonaligned rectangles, so exact comparisons remain difficult.
principles.example: The bridge mosaic emphasizes era-by-material combinations; the US-state treemap nests different states inside four regions.

principles.title: Add counts or percentages when area comparison is difficult
principles.problem: Differently shaped, nonaligned rectangles make equal or similar quantities hard to judge.
principles.solution: Whenever possible, print the relevant counts or percentages on mosaic and treemap regions.
principles.why: Labels let readers verify an impression that the area encoding alone may not support accurately.
principles.applies: Mosaics, treemaps, nested pies, and related area displays.
principles.exceptions: Labels may not fit in very small regions; that limitation can itself motivate another chart form.
principles.example: Figure 11-3 contains equal counts represented by different rectangle shapes, motivating explicit numeric labels.

chapters.title: Visualizing Associations Among Two or More Quantitative Variables
chapters.overview: Moves from scatterplots to multivariate encodings, correlograms, dimension reduction, and paired-data displays.

principles.title: Prefer position over bubble size for quantitative comparison
principles.problem: Small differences in bubble area are hard to see and associations involving the size-mapped variable become obscure.
principles.solution: Use pairwise scatterplots or another position encoding when relationships among quantitative variables are the goal.
principles.why: Wilke states that viewers judge position more accurately than symbol size.
principles.applies: Three or a few quantitative variables.
principles.exceptions: Bubble charts can still give a compact overview when exact associations with the size variable are not central.
principles.example: Figures 12-3 and 12-4 show the same blue-jay variables; the scatterplot matrix reveals relationships hidden by bubble size.

principles.title: Keep raw data available when showing derived association summaries
principles.problem: Correlograms reveal pattern but can hide distributions, outliers, and nonlinear structure.
principles.solution: Prefer raw-data views where feasible or use dimension reduction as a middle ground between raw observations and abstract coefficients.
principles.why: A coefficient matrix can support incorrect conclusions because the underlying points are invisible.
principles.applies: Correlation matrices and high-dimensional quantitative data.
principles.exceptions: For more than three or four variables, all-pairs scatterplots become unwieldy, so a correlogram can be useful as a compact overview.
principles.example: Figures 12-6 and 12-7 summarize glass correlations; PCA views then expose samples in a reduced position space.

principles.title: Use slopegraphs for a few identified paired cases
principles.problem: A scatterplot can hide the identity and direction of change for a small set of paired observations.
principles.solution: Place measurements in columns and connect each case, so line slope shows direction and magnitude.
principles.why: The line creates an explicit within-case comparison and can extend beyond two measurement times.
principles.applies: Small sets of named cases measured at two or more ordered occasions.
principles.exceptions: Scatterplots work better for many points or when the systematic deviation from an equality line is the main message.
principles.example: Figures 12-11 and 12-12 contrast 166-country paired scatter with a labeled 10-country slopegraph.

chapters.title: Visualizing Time Series and Other Functions of an Independent Variable
chapters.overview: Explains when lines express order, how marks affect emphasis, and how to handle multiple or multivariate time series.

sections.title: Multiple Time Series and Dose–Response Curves
Time Series of Two or More Response Variables

principles.title: Connect observations only when an independent variable supplies order
principles.problem: Lines between unrelated points imply interpolation and adjacency that do not exist.
principles.solution: Use lines for time or another naturally ordered independent variable; state that lines guide the eye when interpolation may be misconstrued.
principles.why: Connections visually encode predecessor/successor structure, not additional observations.
principles.applies: Time series and dose–response curves.
principles.exceptions: Sparse, widely separated measurements make the implied interpolation more questionable; a caption qualification can help.
principles.example: Figures 13-1 and 13-2 show bioRxiv monthly observations before and after ordered connections are added.

principles.title: Use points, lines, and fills to control temporal emphasis
principles.problem: Dense points add clutter, while filled areas can imply magnitude from zero.
principles.solution: Drop points when the overall trend is primary and sampling is dense; fill under a curve only with a zero baseline.
principles.why: Removing points deemphasizes individual observations; a filled area strongly separates above from below and encodes value through height.
principles.applies: Dense time series and area charts.
principles.exceptions: Keep points when observations or sampling locations matter; nonzero-baseline area fills are invalid.
principles.example: Figures 13-3 and 13-4 progressively emphasize the bioRxiv trend, with the area chart retaining a zero baseline.

principles.title: Directly label multiple time-series lines when possible
principles.problem: A separate legend forces repeated visual lookup and matching.
principles.solution: Place series names near their lines and remove redundant point shapes or legends.
principles.why: Direct labels reduce cognitive transfer between the legend and data.
principles.applies: A manageable number of line series with separable endpoints or paths.
principles.exceptions: Crowded or crossing series may not leave clean label locations; small multiples may then work better.
principles.example: Figure 13-7 streamlines a three-series preprint chart by labeling lines directly.

principles.title: Show direction and pace in connected scatterplots
principles.problem: A connected path of two response variables can become an uninterpretable scribble.
principles.solution: Add temporal markers plus direction cues such as color progression or arrows.
principles.why: Readers otherwise cannot recover which way the path runs or how quickly it moves.
principles.applies: Connected scatterplots of two variables evolving together.
principles.exceptions: Separate line graphs are usually easier to read; connected scatterplots can be rewarding once readers understand the form.
principles.example: Figure 13-11 is labeled bad because it omits the date markers and color shading used in the preceding version.

chapters.title: Visualizing Trends
chapters.overview: Treats smoothing as model-dependent, favors interpretable functional forms, and uses detrending/decomposition to reveal deviations.

sections.title: Showing Trends with a Defined Functional Form

principles.title: Treat a smoother as a model whose defaults require sensitivity checks
principles.problem: Different smoothing methods and tuning choices can produce different trends, especially at boundaries.
principles.solution: Try multiple reasonable smoothers/settings and disclose or justify the chosen model.
principles.why: Moving averages, LOESS, and spline variants weight data differently; their curves are not neutral summaries.
principles.applies: Scatterplot and time-series smoothing.
principles.exceptions: The best method depends on data size, computation, and analytical purpose; Wilke does not endorse one universal smoother.
principles.example: Figure 14-5 shows LOESS and several spline fits behaving differently on the same fuel-tank data.

principles.title: Prefer an appropriate interpretable functional form when available
principles.problem: General smoothers can behave unpredictably and do not yield parameters with clear meaning.
principles.solution: Fit a scientifically defensible functional form with interpretable parameters; assess transformations that make the relationship linear.
principles.why: A defined form connects the drawn trend to a stated model and enables meaningful parameter interpretation.
principles.applies: Relationships with plausible mechanistic or well-known mathematical form.
principles.exceptions: Do not force a convenient curve when no suitable form is justified; exploratory smoothers remain useful.
principles.example: Figure 14-6 uses a saturating function for fuel-tank capacity; Figures 14-8 and 14-9 compare exponential fitting with a linear fit after log transformation.

principles.title: Detrend when deviations from expectation are the message
principles.problem: A dominant long-term trend can conceal episodic departures.
principles.solution: Show values relative to the estimated long-term trend, or decompose trend, seasonal, and remainder components.
principles.why: Removing the baseline makes unexpected changes visually salient and allows their magnitude to be interpreted relative to expectation.
principles.applies: Long time series with trend or seasonality.
principles.exceptions: The trend estimate is itself a model; retain or pair the original series so the transformation remains interpretable.
principles.example: Figures 14-10 and 14-11 show how detrending reveals California and Nevada housing bubbles.

chapters.title: Visualizing Geospatial Data
chapters.overview: Covers projection and layer choices, choropleth constraints, and cartograms as deliberate geographic distortion.

principles.title: Choose map projection by the property that must be preserved
principles.problem: Flattening the globe necessarily distorts area, angles, shape, distance, or continuity.
principles.solution: Select a projection whose preserved property matches the analytical task and disclose consequential distortions.
principles.why: No flat projection preserves every spatial property; design is an explicit tradeoff.
principles.applies: World and regional maps.
principles.exceptions: Mercator variants remain useful for limited local areas or web navigation despite severe global area distortion.
principles.example: Figures 15-1 to 15-3 contrast orthographic, Mercator, and equal-area interrupted projections.

principles.title: Do not silently rescale relocated map regions
principles.problem: Moving and shrinking an inset changes perceived area while retaining the appearance of a common map.
principles.solution: Keep a consistent area scale or make any rescaling explicit and justified.
principles.why: Readers interpret mapped area quantitatively even when the relocation itself is conventional.
principles.applies: Inset maps and noncontiguous regions.
principles.exceptions: Relocation to reduce empty space is common and useful; the misleading step in Wilke's example is the unfaithful scaling.
principles.example: Figure 15-6 moves and shrinks Alaska to 12% of its true area and is labeled bad; Figure 15-7 relocates without that scaling.

principles.title: Use choropleths primarily for densities, and check area bias
principles.problem: Large regions attract attention and can make non-density quantities appear more prevalent.
principles.solution: Map densities when possible; for other quantities, use choropleths only when regions are comparably sized or small relative to the spatial pattern.
principles.why: Dividing by area counters the perceptual association between larger shaded regions and larger amounts.
principles.applies: Administrative-area thematic maps.
principles.exceptions: Wilke allows cautious non-density choropleths under two stated size/scale conditions.
principles.example: Figure 15-14 lets sparse Alaska dominate median income; Figure 15-15 reweights geography by population in a cartogram.

principles.title: Bin choropleth colors when category recognition matters
principles.problem: Readers struggle to match an exact continuous color to a legend.
principles.solution: Discretize the values into roughly four to six distinct color bins when easy lookup outweighs continuous precision.
principles.why: Distinct colors can be uniquely recognized, trading some numeric detail for more reliable perception.
principles.applies: Choropleths intended for category or range reading.
principles.exceptions: Continuous scales may be visually appealing and appropriate when smooth spatial variation, rather than range lookup, is primary.
principles.example: Figure 15-13 bins US county median income into five groups.

chapters.title: Visualizing Uncertainty
chapters.overview: Contrasts expert-efficient interval displays with frequency, distributional, graded, and animated uncertainty displays.

sections.title: Visualizing the Uncertainty of Point Estimates
Visualizing the Uncertainty of Curve Fits

principles.title: Match uncertainty precision and intuitiveness to the audience
principles.problem: Compact expert conventions such as error bars can be misread by nonexperts.
principles.solution: Use error bars or bands for precise, dense expert communication; consider frequency framing or outcome animation when intuitive grasp matters more.
principles.why: Discrete scenarios make possible outcomes tangible, while interval conventions require statistical knowledge.
principles.applies: Choosing an uncertainty form for scientific versus lay audiences.
principles.exceptions: Intuitive displays may sacrifice precision or data density; no single form dominates every context.
principles.example: Figure 16-1 turns 1%, 10%, and 40% probabilities into grids of possible outcomes.

principles.title: Use a small-to-moderate number of quantile dots
principles.problem: Too many dots merge perceptually into a continuous mass and defeat frequency framing.
principles.solution: Use enough dots to communicate probability without losing their discrete identity.
principles.why: People judge relative frequencies of discrete objects better than areas only while the objects remain individually discriminable.
principles.applies: Quantile dot plots for probability distributions, especially lay communication.
principles.exceptions: Fewer dots reduce numerical precision; Wilke explicitly accepts that tradeoff when it improves perceived meaning.
principles.example: Figure 16-3 compares 50 dots with 10 dots and favors the more immediately readable 10-dot version for the election example.

principles.title: Separate population spread from uncertainty of an estimate
principles.problem: Standard deviation and standard error answer different questions but are often confused.
principles.solution: Identify whether the mark shows variability among observations or precision of a parameter estimate, and label it accordingly.
principles.why: Standard deviation describes population spread; standard error describes the sampling distribution of an estimate.
principles.applies: Points with intervals, group summaries, and captions.
principles.exceptions: Related quantities can be mathematically derived from the same sample, but that does not make their meanings interchangeable.
principles.example: Figures 16-4 and 16-5 distinguish sample observations, mean, standard deviation, standard error, and several confidence intervals.

principles.title: State exactly what every error bar represents
principles.problem: The same visual glyph can mean standard deviation, standard error, or multiple confidence levels.
principles.solution: Name the quantity and confidence level in the caption or legend.
principles.why: Without an explicit definition, readers cannot infer the statistical meaning from appearance.
principles.applies: Every figure with error bars.
principles.exceptions: None stated; Wilke phrases this as a must.
principles.example: Figure 16-5 renders five distinct interval meanings for the same chocolate ratings, demonstrating their visual and conceptual differences.

principles.title: Plot uncertainty for the comparison you actually want to make
principles.problem: Inferring significance from overlap between two separate error bars is unreliable.
principles.solution: Calculate and visualize an interval for the difference itself; assess whether that interval includes zero.
principles.why: Both estimates contribute uncertainty to the difference, and separate intervals do not encode that combined quantity directly.
principles.applies: Pairwise or reference-group comparisons of estimates.
principles.exceptions: Multiplicity adjustments may be required when making several comparisons, as in Wilke's example.
principles.example: Figure 16-8 plots each country's mean chocolate-rating difference from the US with multiplicity-adjusted confidence intervals.

principles.title: Remember that nonlinear-fit uncertainty includes shape, not just vertical displacement
principles.problem: A band around a nonlinear fit can look like the best curve merely moves up and down.
principles.solution: Use graded bands or samples of plausible fitted curves when shape uncertainty matters.
principles.why: Alternative nonlinear fits may be more wiggly and structurally different even when their envelope resembles a conventional band.
principles.applies: Spline and other nonlinear curve fits.
principles.exceptions: Bands remain compact and useful; sampled curves add complexity and should serve the interpretive task.
principles.example: Figure 16-18 contrasts a best-fit spline plus band with equally likely alternative curves.

principles.title: Make hypothetical outcome sequences representative
principles.problem: A small or biased animation sample can imply the wrong outcome frequencies.
principles.solution: Use many outcomes or explicitly verify that displayed outcomes approximate the target distribution; prefer hard switches, fast transitions, or fades over slow morphing.
principles.why: HOPs communicate probability through experienced frequency, so a nonrepresentative sequence directly misstates uncertainty; smooth deformation may impair probability judgment.
principles.applies: Animated hypothetical outcome plots online or in presentations.
principles.exceptions: HOPs do not work in print; the best transition remains partly an open research question.
principles.example: Figures 16-19 and 16-20 schematize sampled chocolate comparisons and alternative spline fits.

chapters.title: The Principle of Proportional Ink
chapters.overview: Requires shaded extent to remain proportional to value and works through linear, logarithmic, and direct-area cases.

principles.title: Keep shaded area proportional to the represented value
principles.problem: A mark's endpoint can show one value while its visible area or length implies another.
principles.solution: Whenever shaded extent encodes a number, make that extent directly proportional to the number.
principles.why: Viewers primarily perceive the extent of bars and filled shapes, so contradictory endpoint and area encodings mislead.
principles.applies: Bars, rectangles, filled areas, pies, treemaps, and other extent-based marks.
principles.exceptions: Position-only marks such as dots do not encode value through their area and can use a restricted axis range.
principles.example: Figures 17-1 and 17-2 compare Hawaiian income bars starting at $50,000 versus zero.

principles.title: Start linear-scale bars and filled amounts at zero
principles.problem: A truncated origin exaggerates the magnitude of differences.
principles.solution: Use zero as the baseline for bars on a linear scale, or plot explicitly defined changes from zero instead of the original amounts.
principles.why: Then bar length and endpoint agree and both encode the same amount.
principles.applies: Linear bar and area charts.
principles.exceptions: It is valid to plot differences or changes as their own quantities; negative changes extend in the opposite direction from zero.
principles.example: Figure 17-5 plots change in county income rather than truncating bars of absolute income.

principles.title: On log axes, use bars for ratios and start them at 1
principles.problem: Amount bars on a log scale have no nonarbitrary zero origin.
principles.solution: Use dots for absolute amounts on log scales; if bars are used, make the data ratios and start the bars at the natural midpoint 1.
principles.why: A log axis encodes multiplication/division, so bar extent from 1 has a coherent ratio interpretation.
principles.applies: Fold changes and relative quantities.
principles.exceptions: A log axis remains useful for position-only amounts spanning orders of magnitude.
principles.example: Figures 17-7 to 17-10 progress from invalid log amount bars to dots and then valid ratio bars relative to Papua New Guinea.

principles.title: Prefer length or position when accurate comparison matters
principles.problem: Even correct area encodings make differences look less pronounced and are judged less accurately.
principles.solution: Use aligned bars or positions instead of pies/treemaps when precise magnitude comparison is the main task.
principles.why: Human perception judges distances more accurately than two-dimensional areas.
principles.applies: Comparing amounts across categories.
principles.exceptions: Pies and treemaps can validly emphasize composition or hierarchy while still satisfying proportional ink.
principles.example: Figures 17-11 to 17-13 compare the same county populations as pie, bars, and treemap.

chapters.title: Handling Overlapping Points
chapters.overview: Escalates from transparency and jitter to binning, contours, and faceting as overlap becomes more severe.

principles.title: Combine transparency with restrained jitter for rounded overlaps
principles.problem: Identical coordinates hide counts and can completely occlude minority groups.
principles.solution: Use partial transparency and a small random displacement to expose stacked observations.
principles.why: Darkness indicates density, while slight displacement makes it evident that multiple points are present.
principles.applies: Moderate datasets with rounding or discrete coordinate values.
principles.exceptions: Transparency alone is not self-explanatory; too much jitter misrepresents the data.
principles.example: Figures 18-1 to 18-4 show hidden car observations, transparency, useful jitter, and excessive jitter.

principles.title: Bin points when individual marks collapse into a dark band
principles.problem: At very large sample sizes, transparency hides sparse extremes while dense regions become undifferentiated.
principles.solution: Aggregate observations into rectangular or hexagonal 2D bins and encode counts by color.
principles.why: Binning converts severe overlap into an explicit density estimate across the plane.
principles.applies: Large scatterplots where local frequency is more important than case identity.
principles.exceptions: Binning loses individual observations and depends on bin size; hexagons modestly improve center-distance geometry over equal-area squares.
principles.example: Figures 18-5 to 18-7 convert more than 100,000 flight departures from points to rectangular and hexagonal bins.

principles.title: Use density contours only when groups are few and separable
principles.problem: Multiple overlapping contour systems can form an unreadable hairball.
principles.solution: Overlay contours for slowly varying densities and at most two or three clearly separated groups; otherwise facet the groups.
principles.why: Contours summarize density effectively only while individual line families can be followed.
principles.applies: Point clouds with smooth density and limited grouping.
principles.exceptions: Strongly overlapping or five-plus groups should be separated into panels.
principles.example: Figures 18-10 to 18-13 contrast workable two-group contours with tangled five-cut diamond contours and a faceted solution.

chapters.title: Common Pitfalls of Color Use
chapters.overview: Limits categorical color load, rejects decorative/rainbow color, and requires color-vision-deficiency-aware testing.

sections.title: Encoding Too Much or Irrelevant Information
Using Nonmonotonic Color Scales to Encode Data Values

principles.title: Limit categorical color to a manageable number
principles.problem: Matching many similar colors between marks and a legend becomes a visual puzzle.
principles.solution: Aim for roughly three to five categories; by eight to ten, use broader groups, direct labels, shapes, or panels instead.
principles.why: The burden is not just color discrimination but remembering and matching each category.
principles.applies: Qualitative palettes and legends.
principles.exceptions: Eight distinguishable colors may be technically available, but task burden can become excessive before the palette itself fails.
principles.example: Figures 19-1 and 19-2 replace 51 state colors with four region colors plus selective direct labels.

principles.title: Do not color for decoration alone
principles.problem: Rainbow-like category coloring adds distraction without information.
principles.solution: Assign color a specific semantic or attentional role and remove it when it serves none.
principles.why: Purposeful color should make a figure easier to read; gratuitous color competes with labels and comparisons.
principles.applies: Bars, points, lines, and filled regions.
principles.exceptions: A visual brand or memorable accent may be legitimate, but it still should not obscure the data.
principles.example: Figure 19-3 gives every state bar a saturated rainbow color with no encoded meaning.

principles.title: Avoid nonmonotonic color scales for ordered values
principles.problem: Uneven lightness, especially in rainbow scales, creates false boundaries and arbitrary emphasis.
principles.solution: Use a perceptually monotonic sequential or balanced diverging scale.
principles.why: Readers perceive lightness changes as magnitude changes; reversals distort the encoded order.
principles.applies: Continuous and ordered quantitative color.
principles.exceptions: A qualitative palette is appropriate for unordered categories because it is not meant to encode magnitude.
principles.example: Figures 19-4 and 19-5 show the rainbow scale's lightness reversals and its arbitrary emphasis around 75%.

principles.title: Test color-vision accessibility at the actual mark size
principles.problem: A nominally CVD-safe palette may fail on thin lines or tiny points.
principles.solution: Use CVD-safe palettes, add redundant encodings where needed, and inspect simulations at the final output size.
principles.why: Color differences become harder to discriminate as marks shrink, and the effect worsens under color-vision deficiency.
principles.applies: Any color-coded scientific figure, especially small multiples and dense line/point plots.
principles.exceptions: Sequential scales with a strong lightness gradient are generally robust, but final-size testing still catches context-specific failures.
principles.example: Figures 19-9 to 19-11 show an accessible diverging palette, Okabe–Ito colors, and size-dependent failures.

chapters.title: Redundant Coding
chapters.overview: Uses multiple channels, perceptually ordered legends, and direct labeling to reduce reliance on color.

principles.title: Do not rely on color alone for key distinctions
principles.problem: Color can fail with similar hues, small marks, grayscale output, or color-vision deficiency.
principles.solution: Encode important groups redundantly with color plus shape, line type, position, or direct annotation.
principles.why: A second channel preserves group identity when color is unavailable or ambiguous.
principles.applies: Categorical points, lines, and legends.
principles.exceptions: Additional channels can add noise; reserve redundancy for distinctions the reader must recover.
principles.example: Figures 20-1 to 20-4 add point shapes to Iris species so even the grayscale simulation remains legible.

principles.title: Order legend entries to match their visual order
principles.problem: Alphabetical legend order can conflict with the top-to-bottom or left-to-right order viewers perceive in the data.
principles.solution: Reorder legend entries to mirror the marks' salient visual sequence.
principles.why: Matching orders reduces search and mental remapping between legend and plot.
principles.applies: Line charts and other figures whose groups form a stable spatial ordering.
principles.exceptions: If series cross heavily and have no stable order, direct labels or another layout may be better.
principles.example: Figures 20-5 and 20-6 reorder four technology companies from their perceived high-to-low curve order.

principles.title: Prefer direct labels when they can replace a lookup legend
principles.problem: Legends make readers shuttle information between separated locations.
principles.solution: Place names or annotated guide marks next to the data they identify.
principles.why: Direct labeling removes the transfer step and keeps identity physically attached to the mark.
principles.applies: A manageable number of lines, clusters, or distributions.
principles.exceptions: Crowding may prevent clean direct labels; omitting a legend without adding direct identification is not a solution.
principles.example: Figures 20-8 to 20-10 directly label stock lines, Iris clusters, and density curves.

principles.title: Integrate legends when one variable uses multiple aesthetics
principles.problem: Separate legends for the same variable fragment a single mapping.
principles.solution: Use one legend-like element that demonstrates all redundant encodings together; integrate it with the axis when position and color encode the same variable.
principles.why: A unified guide makes the shared mapping explicit and removes duplicate interpretive work.
principles.applies: Redundant position/color, color/shape, or similar encodings.
principles.exceptions: Only combine guides that truly represent the same variable and scale.
principles.example: Figure 20-12 embeds the temperature color bar along the temperature position axis.

chapters.title: Multipanel Figures
chapters.overview: Separates small multiples from compound figures and addresses shared scales, panel order, visual language, labeling, and alignment.

principles.title: Keep small-multiple scales consistent
principles.problem: Per-panel rescaling exaggerates small changes and hides differences in absolute magnitude.
principles.solution: Use the same axis ranges and transformations across panels.
principles.why: Readers expect repeated panels to be directly comparable and commonly assume shared scaling.
principles.applies: Faceted plots that repeat the same chart form.
principles.exceptions: If differing scales are unavoidable, call them out explicitly in the caption.
principles.example: Figures 21-3 and 21-4 compare degree trends with free versus common y-axis ranges.

principles.title: Order panels by a logical sequence
principles.problem: Arbitrary facet order makes a multipanel display harder to scan.
principles.solution: Arrange panels by time, natural rank, magnitude, or another task-relevant rule.
principles.why: A coherent sequence creates an expected reading path and exposes patterns across panels.
principles.applies: Small multiples and repeated categories.
principles.exceptions: The rule depends on the intended comparison; no single ordering fits every figure.
principles.example: Wilke orders Titanic classes high-to-low, movie panels chronologically, and degree areas by average popularity.

principles.title: Use one visual language across compound panels
principles.problem: Changing colors, category order, fonts, or symbols between panels makes the same thing look different.
principles.solution: Keep semantic mappings and ordering consistent throughout the compound figure.
principles.why: Consistency lets readers transfer interpretation between panels with little mental effort and may eliminate duplicate legends.
principles.applies: Figures assembled from different plot types or tools.
principles.exceptions: Different quantities may require different chart forms, but shared entities should retain shared appearance.
principles.example: Figures 21-7 and 21-8 contrast inconsistent and consistent sex colors/order in an athlete figure.

principles.title: Keep panel labels subordinate and panels aligned
principles.problem: Oversized labels and slight misalignments make assembled figures look fragmented.
principles.solution: Use unobtrusive, consistent panel labels and align axes and graphical elements precisely.
principles.why: Labels are navigation aids rather than data; alignment makes panels read as one designed object.
principles.applies: Compound figures, especially panels prepared in separate software.
principles.exceptions: Labels must remain legible at final reproduction size.
principles.example: Figure 21-6 shows intrusive labels; Figure 21-9 exaggerates common alignment failures.

chapters.title: Titles, Captions, and Tables
chapters.overview: Assigns titles and captions to publication context, requires explanatory labels and units, and warns against both omission and redundancy.

principles.title: Give every figure one title in the location its medium expects
principles.problem: Missing, duplicated, or misplaced titles weaken the message and conflict with publication layout.
principles.solution: State the figure's point once: in the caption block for conventional articles/books, or integrated into a standalone infographic.
principles.why: A title tells readers what the figure is about, while one authoritative location prevents redundancy and layout conflict.
principles.applies: Manuscripts, reports, web graphics, and social media.
principles.exceptions: Integrated title/subtitle/source text is appropriate when the figure must stand alone without an external caption.
principles.example: Figures 22-1 and 22-2 present the same corruption graphic as a publication figure and a standalone infographic.

principles.title: Label quantitative axes and legends with variables and units
principles.problem: Readers cannot reliably infer what values mean or what measurement units apply.
principles.solution: Name each mapped variable and give units for quantitative measures whenever possible.
principles.why: Explicit mapping removes guesswork and lets the display be interpreted independently of assumptions.
principles.applies: Axes, size/color legends, and any quantitative scale.
principles.exceptions: Titles may be omitted when tick or category labels are fully self-explanatory, such as obvious calendar years.
principles.example: Figure 22-3 labels blue-jay mass, length, skull size, and sex, including units for all numerical variables.

principles.title: Omit labels only when meaning is genuinely obvious
principles.problem: Contextual hints can leave readers nearly—but not completely—certain about an axis.
principles.solution: Retain labels needed for unambiguous interpretation, while removing only clearly redundant titles.
principles.why: A caption rarely maps variables to axes as directly as a label does; uncertainty about meaning interrupts reading.
principles.applies: Minimalist figure design.
principles.exceptions: Overlabeling also adds awkward redundancy, and whole axes may be omitted in inherently axis-free or qualitatively focused displays.
principles.example: Figures 22-4 to 22-6 range from an acceptably omitted year title to an ambiguous y axis and then excessive labeling.

chapters.title: Balance the Data and the Context
chapters.overview: Rejects both clutter and context-free minimalism, with specific guidance for grids, framing, and reference lines.

sections.title: Providing the Appropriate Amount of Context

principles.title: Do not erase the context that anchors the data
principles.problem: Excessive minimalism leaves marks floating, facets undefined, and legends confused with observations.
principles.solution: Add only the framing, background, or guide lines needed to bind elements and support comparison.
principles.why: Non-data ink can establish baselines, group boundaries, and visual unity; removing all of it can reduce comprehension.
principles.applies: Minimalist plots and small multiples.
principles.exceptions: Context must remain subordinate to the data; heavy grids can overpower foreground marks.
principles.example: Figures 23-5 and 23-6 add light facet backgrounds and horizontal guides to a floating Titanic small-multiple display.

principles.title: Use grid lines that support the primary comparison
principles.problem: Full or strongly styled grids can compete with the data without aiding the task.
principles.solution: Choose light guides oriented perpendicular to the key value dimension; omit unhelpful directions.
principles.why: Perpendicular guides provide reference points for reading mark positions or lengths.
principles.applies: Line, bar, dot, and similar axis-based plots.
principles.exceptions: Scatterplots without a primary direction may benefit from a grid in both directions; visual branding can also affect background choice.
principles.example: Figure 23-10 uses thin horizontal guides for stock values, while Figure 23-11 uses vertical guides for horizontal bars.

principles.title: Use the reference line that directly encodes the comparison
principles.problem: A generic grid can obscure deviation from a scientifically meaningful null or equality relation.
principles.solution: Draw the relevant reference—such as x=y for paired data—and remove competing grid detail when it becomes busy.
principles.why: A task-specific line immediately separates above/below or positive/negative deviation.
principles.applies: Paired scatterplots, residuals, thresholds, and null comparisons.
principles.exceptions: Combining a full grid and strong reference line may overwhelm the points; choose the smallest sufficient context.
principles.example: Figures 23-13 to 23-15 compare a diagonal equality line, a generic grid, and an overly busy combination.

chapters.title: Use Larger Axis Labels
chapters.overview: Treats text size as a final-output and whole-figure balance problem rather than a software-default setting.

principles.title: Do not trust default annotation sizes
principles.problem: Software defaults commonly make axes, ticks, and legend text too small for comfortable reading.
principles.solution: Increase annotation sizes and evaluate them in the complete figure.
principles.why: Legibility and visual balance depend on text being commensurate with marks and available space.
principles.applies: Nearly all publication and presentation figures.
principles.exceptions: Larger is not automatically better; oversized text can unbalance a figure.
principles.example: Figures 24-1 to 24-3 progress from barely readable defaults to a balanced athlete scatterplot.

principles.title: Judge text and mark balance at final reproduction size
principles.problem: A figure that looks oversized on screen may become the only legible version after reduction.
principles.solution: Scale the figure to its intended physical/display size and check text, points, and lines together.
principles.why: All elements shrink at reproduction; relative balance determines whether data marks disappear beside labels.
principles.applies: Journal columns, slides, posters, and responsive outputs.
principles.exceptions: If labels must be large, increase the data marks as well rather than changing text alone.
principles.example: Figures 24-4 and 24-5 show that large text becomes acceptable after point sizes are balanced and the figure is reduced to two or three inches.

chapters.title: Avoid Line Drawings
chapters.overview: Prefers solid filled objects over outlines while preserving proportional ink and managing overlap separately.

principles.title: Prefer solid filled shapes to outline-only marks
principles.problem: Outlines can make inside/outside ambiguous, create optical clutter, and weaken the sense of amount.
principles.solution: Use restrained solid fills for bars, histograms, distributions, points, and boxes.
principles.why: Filled regions are perceived as coherent objects and convey area more immediately.
principles.applies: Bars, histograms, density areas, points, and boxplots.
principles.exceptions: The recommendation never overrides proportional ink; fills must still encode quantities faithfully.
principles.example: Figures 25-1 and 25-2 contrast empty and filled Titanic histograms.

principles.title: Use transparent fills when distribution areas overlap
principles.problem: Line-only densities have weak visual presence, while opaque fills hide distributions behind them.
principles.solution: Fill density areas with partial transparency.
principles.why: Shading makes each distribution a distinct object while transparency keeps the others visible.
principles.applies: A small number of overlapping density curves.
principles.exceptions: Many strongly overlapping distributions may still require faceting or another arrangement.
principles.example: Figures 25-3 to 25-5 progress from dashed outlines to colored lines to transparent filled densities.

principles.title: Use solid points and solve overplotting directly
principles.problem: Open and differently outlined symbols create visual noise and have weak presence.
principles.solution: Use solid color-and-shape coding, and address overplotting with the methods from Chapter 18.
principles.why: Filled points separate groups more cleanly and remain usable in grayscale with redundant shape.
principles.applies: Grouped scatterplots.
principles.exceptions: Wilke acknowledges the argument that open centers reveal covered points but judges the noise cost greater in general.
principles.example: Figures 25-6 and 25-7 contrast black-and-white outline symbols with solid color-and-shape coding.

chapters.title: Don't Go 3D
chapters.overview: Rejects decorative and most static positional 3D, while retaining narrow uses for actual 3D objects and interactive/rotating views.

principles.title: Remove 3D that carries no data
principles.problem: Perspective decoration changes apparent sizes and occludes marks without encoding another variable.
principles.solution: Render pies, bars, and lines in ordinary 2D when the third dimension has no substantive role.
principles.why: Projection distorts front and back objects, and the visual system can only partially correct the distortion.
principles.applies: Decorative 3D charts.
principles.exceptions: None for gratuitous 3D; Wilke calls it unequivocally bad.
principles.example: Figures 26-1 and 26-2 show angle-dependent pie slices and distorted Titanic stacked bars.

principles.title: Prefer invertible 2D encodings to static 3D position
principles.problem: A static 2D projection cannot uniquely reveal where points lie in 3D and depends on fragile depth cues.
principles.solution: Use 2D projections, other visual channels, or small multiples.
principles.why: Mapping directly to 2D avoids a second noninvertible transformation from 3D scene to flat display.
principles.applies: Multivariable scatterplots and grouped 3D bars.
principles.exceptions: The objection is primarily to 3D shown on 2D displays; true 3D environments change the perceptual problem.
principles.example: Figures 26-3 to 26-8 replace a 3D car scatterplot and mortality bars with 2D views and small multiples.

principles.title: Use 3D when three-dimensional structure is itself the subject
principles.problem: A blanket prohibition would exclude actual surfaces and objects whose form is intrinsically spatial.
principles.solution: Use 3D for real 3D objects/data, preferably interactively, in VR/AR, or with slow rotation that supplies multiple viewpoints.
principles.why: Multiple views allow the brain to reconstruct spatial structure; a real 3D object makes the extra dimension semantically necessary.
principles.applies: Topography, molecular structures, anatomy, and similar spatial subjects.
principles.exceptions: Static views remain harder to interpret than interactive or rotating ones.
principles.example: Figures 26-9 and 26-10 show Corsica relief and conservation mapped on a protein structure.

chapters.title: Understanding the Most Commonly Used Image File Formats
chapters.overview: Explains vector/raster tradeoffs, compression artifacts, and preservation of master-quality figure files.

sections.title: Lossless and Lossy Compression of Bitmap Graphics

principles.title: Match vector or bitmap storage to figure complexity
principles.problem: Raster figures pixelate when enlarged, while huge vector scenes can render slowly and suffer font substitution.
principles.solution: Use vector output for ordinary plots and line art; consider high-resolution raster output for extremely dense graphics and embed or outline fonts when needed.
principles.why: Vectors preserve geometric sharpness at arbitrary scale, while rasterizing a dense scene bounds file/rendering cost.
principles.applies: Figure export and manuscript production.
principles.exceptions: Bitmaps reproduce identically across systems; vectors depend on rendering software and available fonts.
principles.example: Figure 27-1 magnifies the same image as bitmap and vector to show pixelation versus scale independence.

principles.title: Avoid JPEG for plots, text, and screenshots
principles.problem: Lossy compression creates visible or print-sensitive artifacts around sharp edges.
principles.solution: Use PNG or TIFF for bitmap data visualizations and reserve JPEG for photographic images.
principles.why: JPEG is optimized for photographic gradients, not line art or text; lossless formats preserve exact pixels.
principles.applies: Raster export of scientific figures.
principles.exceptions: JPEG is suitable for photographs; mixed photo-and-text images should still use PNG or TIFF when quality matters.
principles.example: Figure 27-2 shows increasing JPEG artifacts as compression rises.

principles.title: Preserve a maximum-quality master and convert downward
principles.problem: Format conversion cannot restore vector structure, resolution, or detail already lost.
principles.solution: Keep an original PDF/vector or high-resolution lossless bitmap, then downscale or convert copies for delivery.
principles.why: Information loss is one-way: wrapping JPEG in PDF or converting JPEG to PNG does not undo rasterization or artifacts.
principles.applies: Archiving and reproducible publishing workflows.
principles.exceptions: Use the best available source when an original lossless/vector asset does not exist.
principles.example: The chapter's conversion discussion contrasts vector-to-bitmap loss with superficial container changes.

chapters.title: Choosing the Right Visualization Software
chapters.overview: Evaluates tools by reproducibility, exploratory flexibility, presentation control, and separation of content from design.

principles.title: Make the plotted result reproducible and, when needed, repeatable
principles.problem: A figure cannot be regenerated reliably if data, transformations, or random elements are unspecified.
principles.solution: Preserve plotted data and transformations; for pixel-level repetition, also control random generators and seeds.
principles.why: Reproducibility preserves the message, while repeatability recreates the exact appearance including jitter.
principles.applies: Scientific pipelines and figures with random placement.
principles.exceptions: Substantially similar appearance may be enough for reproducibility even when fonts, colors, or jitter differ.
principles.example: Figure 28-1 contrasts an exact repeat of a jittered plot with a reproduction carrying the same information but different design and jitter.

principles.title: Use different criteria for exploration and presentation
principles.problem: A polished but inflexible tool slows exploration, while a fast exploratory plot may be unfit for publication.
principles.solution: During exploration optimize rapid remapping and chart switching; during presentation optimize precise, publication-ready communication.
principles.why: The phases have different objectives: discovering patterns versus conveying a known point.
principles.applies: Tool and workflow selection.
principles.exceptions: One tool may support both phases; switching tools is also reasonable.
principles.example: Wilke contrasts rapid changes among scatterplots, densities, boxplots, and heatmaps with later finalization paths.

principles.title: Separate figure content from reusable design
principles.problem: Entangling data mappings with styling makes consistent redesign and collaboration difficult.
principles.solution: Determine variables, transformations, scales, ranges, and chart type first; apply fonts, colors, grids, and layout as a separate theme or design layer.
principles.why: Separation lets analysts focus on data and designers define a consistent visual language that can be reused.
principles.applies: Code-based figure systems and multi-figure projects.
principles.exceptions: Final design can feed back into content when legibility reveals a structural limitation; the separation is a workflow principle, not an absolute wall.
principles.example: Figure 28-3 applies four themes to the same unemployment time-series content.

chapters.title: Telling a Story and Making a Point
chapters.overview: Frames figures as factual story components, prioritizes message clarity, stages complexity, and balances consistency with memorability.

sections.title: Make a Figure for the Generals
Be Consistent but Don't Be Repetitive

principles.title: Use figure sequence to create a factual question and resolution
principles.problem: A single dense figure may reveal the answer without building understanding or may fail to connect observations into a point.
