principles.solution: Arrange figures so one establishes context or challenge and the next resolves it; compress to one figure only when the medium demands it.
principles.why: Ordered facts create a story arc that guides reasoning and memory without inventing evidence.
principles.applies: Papers, talks, reports, and explanatory posts.
principles.exceptions: A short-attention medium may require a single self-contained figure.
principles.example: Figures 29-1 and 29-2 first show q-bio growth stopping and then reveal the coincident rise of bioRxiv.

principles.title: Remove data dimensions tangential to the intended message
principles.problem: A technically sophisticated figure can bury the conclusion under variables the story does not need.
principles.solution: State the audience and intended point, then keep only the encodings needed to see it quickly.
principles.why: Busy readers cannot spend long deciphering a chart; added dimensions divide attention and can leave no clear takeaway.
principles.applies: Communicative figures after analysis is complete.
principles.exceptions: Exploratory figures may legitimately show more dimensions; supporting analyses can be shown separately.
principles.example: Figures 29-3 to 29-5 replace an overloaded flight-delay bubble/trend plot with two simple bars answering the key questions.

principles.title: Introduce a complex figure through a simple subset
principles.problem: Showing a large multipanel display all at once overloads an audience unfamiliar with its grammar.
principles.solution: First explain one representative panel or subset, then reveal the complete figure.
principles.why: The audience learns the encoding on a small example and can reuse that understanding across the larger display.
principles.applies: Presentations and documents with complex small multiples.
principles.exceptions: A familiar audience or simple figure may not need staged introduction.
principles.example: Figures 29-6 and 29-7 move from one airline/airport weekday pattern to a grid covering ten airlines and three airports.

principles.title: Add distinctiveness without sacrificing quick comprehension
principles.problem: Generic charts blur together, but decorative complexity can make exact reading difficult.
principles.solution: Use a modest, subject-relevant visual device only after clarity is secured.
principles.why: Unique visuals improve memory, yet complexity also slows overview and comparison; the design must balance both effects.
principles.applies: Public communication and sequences of similar figures.
principles.exceptions: A memorable but confusing figure is not a successful data visualization.
principles.example: Figures 29-8 and 29-9 compare a generic pet bar chart with an isotype design using repeated animal images.

principles.title: Keep semantics consistent while varying form across distinct analyses
principles.problem: Identical chart forms can make different findings blur together, even when styling is consistent.
principles.solution: Retain common colors, fonts, and meanings, but select different appropriate chart types for different analytical points.
principles.why: Consistency signals one story; variation helps the audience recognize transitions and remember separate results.
principles.applies: Compound figures, papers, and presentation sequences.
principles.exceptions: Do not vary chart type merely for novelty; each form still has to suit its data and comparison.
principles.example: Figures 29-11 and 29-12 replace a repetitive second stock time series with a bar chart of percent increase.

principles.title: Show raw evidence before increasingly derived summaries
principles.problem: A derived coefficient or percent change can be hard to trust or understand without seeing the observations it summarizes.
principles.solution: Start a figure sequence close to the raw data, then introduce averages, changes, or model coefficients as needed.
principles.why: Raw views are more intuitive; derived views efficiently summarize the key trend after the audience has context.
principles.applies: Multi-figure scientific narratives.
principles.exceptions: Showing every raw detail can become repetitive; the sequence should remain concise and medium-appropriate.
principles.example: Figure 29-12 first shows Facebook's stock trajectory and then compares derived percentage increases across companies.
